entry.title: Poetry
entry.content:
Dear practical friend,

You tell me you want to “get into poetry”. You really don’t have to. But I hope you will allow me, in this letter, to fortify your capacity to entertain the thought if it ever strikes you. You might have read, for instance, Auden’s Funeral Blues (made famous by Four Weddings and a Funeral):

Stop all the clocks, cut off the telephone,
Prevent the dog from barking with a juicy bone,
Silence the pianos and with muffled drum
Bring out the coffin, let the mourners come.

Let aeroplanes circle moaning overhead
Scribbling on the sky the message ‘He is Dead’.
Put crepe bows round the white necks of the public doves,
Let the traffic policemen wear black cotton gloves.

He was my North, my South, my East and West,
My working week and my Sunday rest,
My noon, my midnight, my talk, my song;
I thought that love would last forever: I was wrong.

The stars are not wanted now; put out every one,
Pack up the moon and dismantle the sun,
Pour away the ocean and sweep up the wood;
For nothing now can ever come to any good.

You can also hear Tom Hiddleston reading it, if you’d like. It is practically the standard English poem of grief and mourning. It was heartrending to me the first time I read it, and I acquired a new sense of grief – grief with its child-tyrant resentment towards joy, grief with its totalising dismissal of the possibility of good. The poem, however, was part of The Ascent of F6, a satire about how pompous politicians we barely knew are extravagantly fawned over, how their deaths are made events of national mourning. But we are humourless and unserious in our grief, as one might expect. We are self-important – as self-important as any pompous politician – and grief demands to be treated with respect in the many months before you acquire the capacity to laugh about what once made you weep. And so this is our standard lament.

I am hoping that appreciating how little it takes to move you will make poetry less intimidating. Think about how simple we are, how piano-keyed and pliable, how finely our hearts are strung. I hope this also dispels any notions about what sorts of people tend to become poets, or read poetry. My grandfather is a poet, and this demystified the vocation a great deal for me. I grew up watching poems being written; it was mundane, as were the events that inspired great sonnets. I liked it this way; it seemed like a pleasantly quotidian life. There were no Byronic figures around, and if there were, they were more likely to be deadbeats and delinquents than poets.

That was the practical advice, here comes the romanticism: Poetry can help you access beliefs that you did not know you had – in the uncanniest ways.

When Elizabeth II died, I felt a very confusing sense of gravity, and tried to express this to a very confused friend. “Listen”, I was saying, “I don’t know quite how to say this, but this is all quite sad – like, this is an important moment.” I was stuck trying to explain the importance of a monarch to someone reminding me of the crude violations against justice and goodness committed in English history.

And then Auden’s Death’s Echo popped into my head:

The desires of the heart are as crooked as corkscrews,
Not to be born is the best for man;
The second-best is a formal order,
The dance’s pattern; dance while you can.

Dance, dance for the figure is easy,
The tune is catching and will not stop;
Dance till the stars come down from the rafters;
Dance, dance, dance till you drop.

I eventually wrote an essay, originally titled “The second best is a formal order”, which begins with these verses, to explain how I felt to my friend. All of this is to say: the mind is a strange thing and you never know what will remind you of what. The great poems you read will be allusions in your head, phrases that can fill all sorts of events with meaning, pitch, timbre. They can make the world “thicker”, in the sense that blood is thicker than water.

Yours sincerely,
Nihal

Was fun to revisit everything again, and I almost got inspired to start a big project. Maybe once I’m back in Bengaluru!

Raft shenanigans continued, and we’re finally making progress towards the actual story instead of just aimless wandering.

Work

I took last Friday and this Monday off work to have a relaxing long weekend at home but boredom got the better of me by Monday and I couldn’t help but check on things and get a bit of work done. Hopefully we’ll be able to make the much needed additions to our team sooner than later.

Personal Projects

Claw had a bunch of changes this week. I reorganized the entire codebase to more closely follow the Android multi-module guidance, going from 10 modules to 37 as of writing. The previous module layout was inherited from the app’s past as Kotlin Multiplatform app which had become messy and cumbersome in the 5 years since. It’s also a chance for me to get some practical experience with taming a decently sized Gradle build (relatively speaking, Cash App’s has 800+ modules) and learn how things like compilation avoidance and cache invalidation work in these scenarios.

I also cut out the Haze backed fancy navigation bar and replaced it with the standard Material3 one.

Another UI change that landed this week was adding a small shared element transition going from a post to its comments page, which uncovered a regression in the Navigation3 library.

Some homelab changes: I swapped out my webmail from alps to pl_mail, and quite love it. It supports WebDAV + CalDAV, SSO, and just works much better in general. There are obvious downsides in the form of PHP and it being complete slop, but alps is just as bad so I’ve made peace with the fact that selfhosted webmail can either be ancient or slop. To minimize risk I’ve kept pl_mail in its containerized format instead of directly running it on the host, and kept it restricted to my Tailscale network.

entry.title: Implementing An RSS Feed Generator For This Site
entry.content:
I began attending IndieWebClub Bangalore meetups last month. They're fun, and I'll gush about them later. I've got a particularly hilarious comparison to make with another impressive group I've joined around the same time.

The point of this post is the work I did on the 30th of October to get included into their members directory.

Criteria

To get included on the IWCB members page, there are some criteria one has to meet:

  • Attend in-person sessions: check
  • Have a blog: check
  • Have an RSS feed on the blog: I mean… I'll implement one some dayyyy, ugh fine I'll do it now

The Thinking

Well, how tough could implementing an RSS feed be? There are probably a hundred and one plugins in Flask that'll do that for you, but I didn't want a plugin. I wanted this website to be purely handmade (well, as best as I could), so I decided to write a feed generator custom-built for my site. The way my blog was set up, I'd really have to struggle with XPath to get the feed through FreshRSS too.

So, writing a feed generator it was. Through work, I've already had experience with the BeautifulSoup library which handles HTML and XML documents. This meant I didn't have to perform string manipulation directly, which (from experience) promised to get real tiring real fast.

The feeds I already followed didn't have a common template. I know now that the difference was between Atom feeds and RSS feeds (a friend pointed out on the 3rd of November that XKCD implemented both), but I only knew RSS on the day I was motivated to implement it all.

Wikipedia listed https://www.rssboard.org/ as the official website of the RSS spec, so there I went. They had an RSS feed for their own blog linked in the sidebar. I was going to go click on it, but the link to the specification caught my eye and I had to check it out.
It was short but very dry and could not hold my attention. But wait, they linked to a page listing best practices for RSS feeds! And while this page contained more information than the spec, it's broken down into neat little sections that felt way more actionable.

The Doing

I started out with a blank Soup object

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
soup = BeautifulSoup(features="xml")

to which I then added the top level rss tag, with the version attribute, and then the channel tag as a child tag

soup.append(soup.new_tag("rss", version="2.0))
rss = soup.rss
rss.append(rss.new_tag("channel"))

Then to the rss tag, I went about adding the metadata children tags

channel = rss.channel
for name, string in children.items:
    channel.append(channel.new_tag(name))
    channel.findall(name)[-1].string = string

This way, I could define a dictionary with the tags and their content strings to insert in one go. Of course, this meant I couldn't add any tags with attributes, but I cleverly solved that problem by not implementing any tags with attributes.

At this point, I could paste my feed in the feed validator to fix any mistakes. Finally came the item tags, each one representing one blog post. I could get all the posts from the database as a list, reverse the order (to have the recent posts at the top of the feed even though the order of the items is meaningless according to the spec), and insert the child tags for each item tag.

One thing I got lucky with was HTML escaping. To avoid confusing HTML tags and XML tags, the HTML in the blog post content must be escaped - I must use < and > instead of < and >. Thankfully, BeautifulSoup handled that implicitly for me.

The Integrating

Finally, I just set my blog up to update the feed and write it to a file every time I created, edited, or deleted a post. Then, I made the desired permanent link redirect to the static file, whose location may or may not change later.

entry.title: The slow death of a web browser
entry.content:
And the long search for a new one.

A few weeks ago, The Browser Company announced that it is shutting down Arc.

For anyone who has barely noticed, this was not a surprising update. Arc had long been on life support, receiving only security-patch updates since the company launched its second browser. Meanwhile, dozens of Arc-inspired browsers were chipping away at its once-loyal but now-infuriated customer base. The Arc-inspired dupes scene got so intense that The Browser Company ended up making Dia a dupe too.

Even though my usage of Arc paused the moment the Dia announcement dropped, the news about the browser shutting down for good brought up a lot of feelings for me. It was not a surprise, but there was also sadness for what was lost. Arc felt like the first glimpse into something truly unique and great, but also a dream that never fully manifested.

One good thing did come out of it, though. It helped move the rest of the browser industry forward. Over the last couple of years, it opened up the new possibilities of what a browser could be and challenged users to demand more of their browsers.

The browser is the most important application anyone can have on their computer. Irrespective of the work you do, you probably use one constantly. Browsers have become so capable over time that almost any task imaginable can now happen inside of a tab. Along with your regular browsing and organising your links better than ever before, you can now design, and even code in your browsers. Some are even cosplaying as full-on operating systems. Might not be the most efficient way to do something, but you still can do it!

This is why I believe everyone should care a little (a lot) more about the browser they use, probably as much as they care about the operating system on their devices.

Arc was the browser that made me care about mine. My love affair with Arc started the day I encountered those vertical tabs. Immediately, it made me reconsider what a browser could do. Other browsers had vertical tabs for a long time, but Arc’s implementation was just a little more thoughtful. With the pinned tabs and folders, it was not just another feature begrudgingly slapped onto the browser. The same held true of other features like Spaces and quick searches on other websites directly from the command bar. These were not entirely new ideas, but definitely more mindful implementations.

What made Arc such a joy to use was how it made the web feel like a place I could explore again, rather than struggle through a stream of pages, trying to pass through.

Arc’s influence is visible in other browsers today too. Despite its near-total market dominance, Chrome added features that actually make it more useful, sometimes even against the wishes of its Search team. More browsers now support tab groups and vertical tabs. Even Safari added vertical tabs. Safari, who would have thunk!

As Arc’s development slowed down, I found myself doing some intense soul-searching to find the new perfect browser for me. Around that time, nearly everyone had the same idea for what the future of browsers could be — AI. Perplexity had Comet, The Browser Company pivoted to Dia, and OpenAI, too, decided to care about browsers for a couple of weeks with Atlas. But none of them felt quite the same. After all these detours, I even went back to short stints with Vivaldi, Firefox and Chrome. Maybe lightning could strike twice?

All this searching and trying dozens of browsers, sometimes switching between multiple ones within a week, gave me a lot of clarity on what I wanted a browser to be for me.

I use my phone’s browser very differently from the one on my desktop. On my phone, it is purely a browsing and reading machine. Things like syncing, bookmarks and tab groups do not matter at all. If I want to save something, it goes to my existing workflow. My mobile browser is just a utility that comes along with me. On desktop, it is a completely different story. The browser has to feel like a home I have decorated myself. I want to keep coming back to it, find things I have stored, use them, rearrange them and explore them through a system that only makes sense to me.

I have had better luck finding a browser for my phone. Quiche has been my primary mobile browser for nearly two years now, and it has been nothing short of great. It has a clean design and snappy performance, but the best feature probably is that it does not make you think about itself. Recently, though, I upgraded to Lens, a lightweight browser that builds on many of the good ideas of Arc Search and adds some powerful developer tools on top of it. My favourite being the ability to instantly find out which fonts any webpage is using.

Meanwhile, on the desktop, I have currently given in to using Dia. Living with it for now, still asking myself whether a browser will ever make me feel the same way Arc did. Dia has also ported over many of the useful features from Arc, but what is desperately missing are fresh ideas about what a browser as an operating system could be. An idea that originated from The Browser Company in the first place. With the Atlassian acquisition, I do not know if that vision will ever come true. Or perhaps the dream is to build a Jira operating system? The horror!

Using Dia daily, I know this is not the desktop browser for me in the long term. I just do not feel the same joy I feel while using Lens, or used to with Arc. In case you have any suggestions for a good browser to explore, hit me up.

I want to ask you a few questions too. How do you browse? How do you access the internet? Is it the same across all your devices? I want you to find the perfect browser for yourself, because I believe it is the most important application on your computer.

entry.title: Super Breakfast
entry.content:
Super Breakfast

This blog is about a simple recipe which is super close to my heart.

Imagine this: you wake up on a Sunday morning starving for some good, healthy food. You have a long day ahead. First, you need to go and climb. A session can range anywhere from 5-6 hours to 10-12 hours depending on the day and mood. You'll' skip lunch cause lunch time would be just after you complete your warm-up. And regardless, you can't climb after having lunch. Your next meal you are going to have is at 21:00. You need energy to climb whole day and sustain till the evening!

If you haven't guessed it yet, this is my usual Sunday routine. To sustain this, I need a breakfast which keeps my tummy full and body brimming with energy. It definitely needs to be attractive to my taste buds and also healthy. I achieve this with a breakfast bowl, which is my take on overnight oats. It took quite a bit of experimentation and FAFO-ing to land on a recipe which ticks all the boxes.

To keep myself full, I need something which body digests slowly, solution? Oats. I add protein powder to it, and body needs some fiber to go along with it, solution? Oats. Oats add some protein to the meal themselves, so what's the best base ingredient? Oats.

I need a soaking agent(?) of sorts to soften the oats. I prefer milk. It's easier to add protein powder and fruit to it. This combination is already sweet enough, but if you are craving more sweetness, honey is a good option. I add it regardless, cause HEALTHY!!

Next up, we have peanut butter, cause who can deny more protein? More protein needs more fiber, so let's throw some basil seeds in there. That is followed by a bunch of nuts. I prefer walnuts and almonds over others.

And finally, a bunch of fruits. My usual suspects are bananas, apples and blueberries. I usually switch them with some seasonal alternatives to keep things interesting.

Here's a handy list:

  • oats
  • protein powder
  • milk
  • honey
  • peanut butter
  • nuts
  • bananas
  • apples
  • blueberries
  • basil seeds

Preparation

NOTE: Quantities reflect my preferences, change them according to your needs.

Start by adding half a litre of milk and one scoop (24g) of protein powder to a shaker. Shake aggressively till you get a smooth mixture. In the past, I used to add coffee with unflavoured protein powder. That combination works pretty well too! Now, add four tablespoon of oats to the milk base.

Next, take two to three tablespoons of peanut butter. I prefer the crunchy alternative with broken peanuts over the smooth variety. Make sure to mix the butter properly. It loves to stay with its mates, trapping oats around it and forming a weird lump. Definitely not delightful to get a full lump in the middle of mmmmmm.

Add one tablespoon of honey to it and make sure this to mix it thoroughly too. Next up, add as many nuts as you like. In the past, I have experimented with dried dates, dried figs and cashews. Sadly, none of them stuck around. I want to experiment with pumpkin seeds at some point.

Next up, we have our beloved fruits! The biggest complaint I have heard here is about bananas, some people hate how overpowering their taste is in milk. Personally, I love it. My go-to combination is half a banana, a few diced slices of apples and two or three blueberries. I stay conservative on blueberry side cause I find their taste overpowering and kinda yucky when there are too many of them in milk.

Pack everything in a jar and leave it in the fridge overnight. On the side, take a tablespoon of basil seeds and add just enough water to it. It should be just enough for basil seeds to soak it all up and become their evolved(?) version. Anything less, and they taste super weird. Anything more, and it dilutes the bowl wayyy too much. I have started using strainers recently to escape this measurement hell.

Next morning, empty the jar in a nice bowl and add the soaked basil seeds to it. Voila, we are done 🎉.

I know these photos are bad, but that's all I have right now 🙈. Maybe in my next incarnation, I'll wake up a better food blogger :P.

If you think people should do only what they like after they retire, then I am retired, or I think I’ll never retire; I just keep working. I would always like to learn, build, write, and have fun. I’ll keep doing these things for as long as possible.

Echo has a UTI; he needed care and a visit to the doctor. Pathu is scared of crackers, so somebody needs to be with her all the time. I think we are never out of parental duties.
